newsitem.title: UK: Mark snoozes on Euro crosses, softens elsewhere.
newsitem.headline: Mark snoozes on Euro crosses, softens elsewhere.

text.p: The mark idled in narrow ranges on the bulk of its European cross rates Thursday but both the mark and the continental European bloc in general continued to weaken against the dollar, sterling and yen.

The market currently expects interest rate increases in 1997 in the UK, U.S. and Japan -- and probably in that chronological order, analysts said. Few, if any, expect interest rates to go up this year on continental Europe.
Concerns about the make-up and stability of the new European single currency, meantime, continue to keep investors shy of Europe for now at least, they said.

The dollar set a new 40-month high against the German unit at 1.7566 marks during the European session, sterling bounded to a 61-month high overnight at 2.9430 and mark/yen skidded to its lowest levels since the 20-month trough at 64.66 in early June.

Traders said the daily barrage of official comments on European monetary union continued to point to the project starting on time in 1999 with a broad-based memebership and reasonably flexible interpretation of the entry criteria.
This central market assumption is depressing the mark because it has created jitters about how the new euro, which will replace the German unit, will trade after launch.

"People's basic assumptions about EMU remain the same and I'm not sure the debate about the finer details of the French and German budgets are enough to change that at the moment," said Adrian Schmidt, economist at Chase Manhattan Bank.
French finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Thursday the 1997 French deficit/output ratio could be significantly higher than the 3.0 percent forecast in the 1997 finance bill.
However, he said he hoped the audit of public finances would show a deficit currently as low as 3.4 percent and France must be able to cut the deficit by "a few decimal points" if needed.

"I think most people are looking at the French deficit from a starting position of 3.4/3.5 pct (of GDP) and the French are in a much better position than the Germans to find money under the floorboards to bridge the gaps," said Schmidt at Chase.

Luxembourg's Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker said he is vetoing what he called "this German interpretation" that the treaty demands deficits to be 3.0 percent exactly for EMU. "It (the treaty) is rich as far as interpretation goes," he said.
Speculation of a broad-based EMU were reinforced, meantime, as Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi and his foreign minister Lamberto Dini said they were confident of starting EMU in 1999.
The 10-year yield spread between Italian and German bonds sank to a new record low of 104 basis points in early trade.
At 1050 GMT, mark/lira was trading at 973.00/30 compared with 973.20/40 late Wednesday. Mark/French franc was at 3.3688/91 compared with 3.3685/88 late yesterday.

"The soft EMU story is being used to explain mark weakness and is a convenient excuse for yield-chasers to stay well clear of the continent for the time being," said a trader at a French bank in London.
The prospect of low German interest rates persisting was helped by the latest German economic data, meantime.
German industrial orders broke a four-month uptrend and fell a bigger-than-expected 0.8 percent in May, backing up the picture of a weak industrial production report on Wednesday.
Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said he saw no sign of inflation pressures and no need to change German interest rates at present.

Elsewhere, the market was focusing on the release later today of the June U.S. employment report. The Federal Open Market Committee left interest rates unchanged after its meeting this week but analysts expect a rate rise later this year.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
